articleBlocks: The first four clues look like they belong to different worlds: Pole and Kiwi could be fruits or plants, Dane could be a dog, Thai could be a cuisine. That surface spread is the puzzle's main misdirection. Each word has a loud everyday meaning that drowns out the quieter nationality reading. Pole is a stick or a bean. Kiwi is a fruit or a bird.
Dane is a dog breed. Thai is a menu category.
Chilean is a wine or a fish.
None of those directions cover all five clues. The set only locks when every word is read as a person from a specific country.
The turning point is Thai, because it is almost impossible to read Thai as anything other than a nationality word once the other clues are nearby.
Once Thai is read as a person from Thailand, Dane stops being a dog and becomes a person from Denmark.
Pole stops being a stick and becomes a person from Poland. Kiwi stops being a fruit and becomes a New Zealander.
Chilean stops being a fish and becomes a person from Chile.
The clean final read is not country names but demonyms: Pole, Kiwi, Dane, Thai, Chilean.
That precision matters. The answer is not Poland or Denmark or New Zealand.
It is the person-noun form for each country.
The puzzle works because every clue is a single word that doubles as an everyday object or food, and the nationality meaning is the less obvious one.
solutionNarrative: Pole and Kiwi first pulled me toward fruit nicknames, so that was the first path I tested. It held together for a moment, but dane never really fit it. The more I pushed that first read, the more the board sounded stitched together instead of naturally solved.

The solve turned when I stopped treating dane as just another clue and asked what kind of thing each clue could really be describing. I was no longer trying to rescue fruit nicknames; I was checking whether Pole and Kiwi could survive the same tighter read.

Then I used Dane, Thai, and Chilean as the confirmation round. Dane, Thai, and Chilean stayed inside the real category, so the answer felt earned instead of guessed. The answer was Common national demonyms (i.e., names for people from a specific country).
